medical.title: Why do people still get polio in some countries and not in others?
medical.summary: On a busy street in Karachi, Pakistan, a health care worker kneels down so she's eye to eye with a toddler. She squeezes two drops of liquid onto the child's tongue. Then she takes out a purple marker and colors the child's pinkie fingernail so everyone can see that this toddler is now vaccinated against polio.

medical.title: Adventurous play linked to better physical and mental health in children
medical.summary: The biggest international study ever on risky play has found that children who have more opportunities for outdoor adventurous play tend to have better physical and mental health, as well as improved social and cognitive development.

medical.title: Exploring how autism reduces sensitivity to feedback on decisions
medical.summary: Some people who have autism spectrum disorder struggle to adapt to changing demands in their environment. In a new study in JNeurosci, researchers discovered this struggle may be because these individuals are less sensitive to feedback about their behavior than individuals who do not have autism. This work was led by Nathaniel Zuk at Nottingham Trent University and Jaroslav Slobodskoy-Plusnin at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in collaboration with colleagues at University College London and Hebrew University.

medical.title: Chest 'digital twin' predicts light paths to help plan personalized pneumonia treatment
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) in Brazil and their international collaborators have created a computational model that can generate a "digital twin" of the human thorax. The goal is to personalize the treatment of respiratory diseases using a special type of light.

medical.title: Detailed brain map reveals how the insula shapes bodily sensations and processes pain
medical.summary: Tucked deep within the human brain's lateral fissure, beneath layers of the cerebral cortex, lies the insula. It is the hub that controls sensations ranging from pain and physical touch to hunger and emotions. Yet, it remains an enigma that neuroscientists have been trying to crack for ages. A recent study published in Nature has presented a new, detailed picture of certain regions of the insula that not only provides a new perspective but also questions some older ones.

medical.title: Metabolic vulnerability identified in small cell lung cancer
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Cologne have demonstrated that, while various cellular states of small cell lung cancer are equally dependent on the amino acid cysteine, they react differently when deprived of it. While some cancer cells subsequently die via ferroptosis—a form of cell death in which harmful oxidized fats accumulate in the cell membranes—others undergo apoptosis, a controlled, programmed form of cell death.

medical.title: Wireless neural chip tracks brain changes in real time after Alzheimer's drug administration
medical.summary: A joint research team led by KAIST has used a small, implantable neural chip to wirelessly monitor real-time changes in a neurotransmitter involved in memory and learning after an Alzheimer's drug has been administered. In miniature pigs (minipigs), the team observed an increase in the neurotransmitter signal following drug administration, followed by a gradual return to baseline. The technology could help researchers assess how drugs act in the brain and develop stimulation methods that adapt to the brain's response.

medical.title: Reproductive health and cystic fibrosis: New guidance offers options and hope
medical.summary: For much of the history of cystic fibrosis (CF) care, reproductive health was not a major part of the conversation. Fertility challenges were the norm for men and women with this genetic disorder, and many grew up assuming biological parenthood was not possible.

medical.title: Black patients can face longer breast cancer care delays, study finds
medical.summary: Black patients and people with a learning disability face longer waiting times at key stages of breast cancer care, according to a nationwide study led by the University of Surrey.

medical.title: AI-based computer model offers new weapon against hard-to-treat cancers
medical.summary: In a new paper published in Cell Reports Medicine, the UCL team outlines how they, in collaboration with a University of Cambridge team, developed a new type of treatment-predicting computer program that uses an individual's detailed genetic fingerprint to explore which treatments, if any, may kill their cancer—especially when standard treatments have failed.

medical.title: AI could help identify people at higher risk of common cancers using routine health data
medical.summary: Machine learning models using routinely collected health information, such as blood tests, medical history and lifestyle factors, could help identify people at higher risk of several common cancers, according to an international study reported at the ESMO Congress 2026.

medical.title: Immunotherapy combination extends survival in advanced endometrial cancer
medical.summary: An immunotherapy-based regimen combining durvalumab and the PARP inhibitor olaparib demonstrated encouraging long-term survival outcomes for patients with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer, according to new trial results presented by researchers from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

medical.title: Remission achievable with usual care for axial spondyloarthritis
medical.summary: For patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), remission is attainable with usual care, according to a study published in the Journal of Rheumatology.

medical.title: Heart drug combo reduces kidney damage in septic shock surgery, major trial finds
medical.summary: A simple adjustment to drugs given during operations for septic shock could prevent thousands of patients from suffering kidney damage, according to the results of a major trial now published in JAMA. Scientists from the University of Southampton working with experts from Zhejiang University School of Medicine in China discovered that combining the medications dobutamine and norepinephrine during surgery can significantly lower the risk of acute kidney injury.

medical.title: Implantable device uses ultrasound to improve drug delivery to the brain
medical.summary: Patients with glioblastoma, an aggressive type of brain tumor, usually undergo surgery to remove the tumor. However, it's difficult for surgeons to remove all of the cancer cells, and the tumor often recurs.

medical.title: Patient-reported outcomes worse for patients with rheumatoid arthritis discontinuing TNF inhibitor
medical.summary: For patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), patient-reported outcomes (PROs) generally worsen shortly after tumor necrosis factor inhibitor (TNFi) discontinuation, according to a study published in the Journal of Rheumatology.

medical.title: Next-generation drug reduces endometrial cancer progression and death in trial
medical.summary: A new drug is effective at decreasing the recurrence of, and death from, endometrial cancer, an international study shows. The drug, called sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT), attaches to a protein on the surface of tumor cells and then delivers a targeted dose of a chemical that leads to cancer cell death.

medical.title: Trust and inclusive language key to effective vaccination campaigns, report finds
medical.summary: Public health leaders should invest in long-term work with communities to develop trust and support more effective vaccination communications, according to a new report analyzing London's Why We Get Vaccinated campaign.

medical.title: Study finds links between low levels of lead exposure and strep throat in children
medical.summary: Even low levels of lead exposure can increase the risk of strep throat in children, according to new research from the University at Buffalo.

medical.title: Most pregnancies after living kidney donation are uncomplicated, study finds
medical.summary: Most pregnancies after living kidney donation are uncomplicated, according to a new Canadian study that provides a clearer picture of pregnancy outcomes among kidney donors. The study, published in JAMA and led by researchers at Western University and London Health Sciences Center Research Institute (LHSCRI), compared pregnancies among living kidney donors in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia with those of women in similarly good health who had not donated.

medical.title: Five ways to look after yourself as winter approaches
medical.summary: When the clocks "fall back" in the fall, it signals the start of the winter months. And for many, this time change also signals the start of a difficult period—when the cold weather and long nights wear on their mental health.

medical.title: Treatment revives old liver cells in lab study, may help prevent Alzheimer's and heart disease
medical.summary: The liver's job of clearing harmful substances from the body is so essential that the organ may have implications for addressing unexpected diseases, including Alzheimer's and heart disease. A promising example comes from new Keck School of Medicine of USC research published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry.

medical.title: New zebrafish models could help test treatments for mental health conditions
medical.summary: A humble fish can experience features of mental health conditions such as schizophrenia and autism, raising the possibility that some of our most complex social behaviors may be more deeply encoded in our DNA than previously thought.

medical.title: Adding abiraterone to ADT and docetaxel improves survival in metastatic prostate cancer
medical.summary: Adding abiraterone to standard treatment provides a lasting survival benefit for men whose prostate cancer has already spread at diagnosis, reinforcing the value of early treatment intensification. The findings come from almost eight years of follow-up in the academically led phase 3 PEACE-1 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026.

medical.title: Omega-3 EPA linked to longer survival after surgery for colorectal cancer liver metastases
medical.summary: Patients assigned to receive high-dose eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), an omega-3 fatty acid, before and after surgery for colorectal cancer liver metastases had longer overall survival than those assigned to receive placebo, according to results of the phase 3 EMT2 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026, held in Madrid Oct. 23–27.

science.title: Interfacial intelligence: A new way to design polymer brushes
science.summary: Polymer brushes are dense layers of polymer chains that can be engineered to change how a surface interacts with its surroundings. By controlling interactions with water, ions, proteins and other materials, they can reduce friction, prevent unwanted materials from sticking, improve separation and support the functionality of sensors and other devices.

science.title: Fractional calculus helps 1D model mimic correlations seen in 2D phase transitions
science.summary: Phase transitions are strongly constrained by spatial dimension. In conventional one-dimensional systems with short-range interactions, thermal fluctuations generally prevent continuous degrees of freedom from maintaining order over long distances.

science.title: Clouds on a lava planet challenge what astronomers expected
science.summary: A rocky lava planet once thought to be too extreme to have an atmosphere appears to be wrapped in one with a reflective layer of vaporized silicate mineral clouds, the same family of compounds that make up quartz and sand.

science.title: NASA Invites Media to Moon Landing Simulation Experience in California
science.summary: Members of the media are invited to tour a new lunar landing simulator at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley on Thursday, Oct. 29, and Friday, Oct. 30.

science.title: Emotional content can improve how people process conversations
science.summary: New in JNeurosci, Pyry Heikkinen and colleagues, from the University of Helsinki, explored how emotional meaning influences the way the human brain prioritizes information during naturally spoken conversations in a cocktail party setting.

science.title: Laser-blasted plasma shows how instabilities could heat the sun's corona
science.summary: From its visible surface, the sun radiates heat at a relatively cool temperature of 5,800 Kelvin. Yet within the thin outer layer of the sun's atmosphere known as the corona, electrons can reach temperatures of millions of degrees, for reasons astronomers have yet to fully explain.

science.title: World-famous or local legend? New study investigates global and local forms of collective memory and group identity
science.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte and Bernardo O'Higgins: two 19th-century military leaders renowned to this day in their native countries of France and Chile. Yet, while Napoleon's name and exploits are known throughout the world, O'Higgins remains largely obscure outside his homeland. This phenomenon demonstrates the distinction between global and local collective memory—the shared knowledge of the past that shapes group identity—and it is the topic of newly published research from Constructor University's Professor Dr. Mariana Macedo together with Dr. Melanie Oyarzun, Professor Dr. Cristian Candia and Professor Dr. César A. Hidalgo.

science.title: Lizard tail preserved in amber sheds light on a 100-million-year-old defense mechanism
science.summary: A lizard making a dramatic escape, leaving its tail wriggling behind as it darts to safety, is an image familiar to many. Tail-shedding is one of the most widespread defenses against predators among living lizards, yet tracing the origins of this extraordinary ability has proved to be surprisingly difficult—how can we tell when this escape tactic first arose in lizards?

science.title: Britain's 1972 school reform may have lowered dementia diagnoses half a century later
science.summary: A new study provides perhaps the strongest evidence yet that education can help mitigate long-term dementia risk.

science.title: Japan's largest marine DNA study detects 126 fish species farther north than previously recorded
science.summary: As climate change reshapes habitats both on land and at sea, you might go to the beach one day, only to find yourself in a place that looks nothing like you remember, around sea creatures you don't recognize.

science.title: Armored amphibian lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago, fossils suggest
science.summary: Scientists report fossil evidence of the first fully marine amphibian in a study from the University of California, Davis; Peking University; and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. The amphibian is an armored, giant salamander–sized, bottom-dwelling ocean creature that the researchers named Gerrothorax maritimus.

science.title: Physicists reveal new paradigm for fiber growth in neurodegenerative diseases
science.summary: Some proteins that are linked to neurodegenerative diseases can form both liquid droplets and amyloid fibers. But how are these two states connected, and where do the fibers grow? Leiden physicists Liru Feng and Louise Jawerth have discovered a counter-intuitive mechanism.

science.title: An American startup wants to sell sunlight after dark. Who gets a say?
science.summary: A U.S. startup has booked two Indian rocket launches to test a planned service no company has sold before: sunlight at night.

science.title: Mapping the hidden global labor powering AI
science.summary: Most people know by now that artificial intelligence powers much of the online world, sifting through social media posts, planning driving routes or helping to choose a movie to watch. But what goes largely unseen is the human labor—often performed by people working for low wages in the Global South—that makes this careful algorithmic lifestyle curation possible.

science.title: NASA’s X-59 Aircraft and Test Pilot
science.summary: NASA test pilot Mike Lippert poses for a photo ahead of his first time flying the agency’s X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft on Oct. 21, 2026. The X-59 has flown numerous times since its inaugural flight in November 2025; its first supersonic flight was on June 5, 2026. Lippert took off from NASA’s Armstrong Flight […]

science.title: Sediment core reveals volcanic eruption preceded ancient cold spell by about 150 years
science.summary: A new study led by an international research team including scientists at the University of South Carolina challenges the idea that the ancient Laacher See volcanic eruption in western Europe triggered a significant climate-cooling period affecting central Europe and the Arctic nearly 13,000 years ago.

science.title: While some eucalypts are hard to kill, climate change may test the ability of others to survive
science.summary: There's no tree like the humble eucalypt.

science.title: Stellar collisions may have been common when the universe was young
science.summary: In our solar system's corner of the galaxy, stars rarely collide. It makes sense: Space is vast, and stars have room to roam. Even in most of the present-day universe, stellar collisions are rare. The James Webb Space Telescope, however, peers deep enough into space to see the universe as it was not too long after the Big Bang. Its observations have revealed extraordinarily compact stellar systems, raising the possibility that collisions between stars were once much more common.

science.title: Plants may switch between reproductive strategies more easily than thought
science.summary: When it comes to reproduction, plants have options. Some can fertilize themselves, while others rely on pollen from genetically different plants. Many populations even contain a mixture of both strategies. But scientists have long debated whether this mixed approach is truly stable or simply a temporary stage on the way from one reproductive strategy to another.

science.title: Brain stimulation temporarily changes perception of sexualized images of women
science.summary: Applying mild electrical stimulation to the brain temporarily removed a perceptual bias linked to the sexual objectification of women, in the first study of its kind. The study is published in the journal Social Neuroscience.

science.title: RNA archiving method reveals what a cell did days ago
science.summary: Information on what a cell did a few hours or days ago is generally unavailable to researchers, who can only measure the cell's current status. This is a problem if the aim is to understand how immune responses arise or why individual cancer cells survive treatment.

science.title: Diamond defects confirm 80-year-old theory of crystal stress
science.summary: For the first time, researchers in Japan have directly mapped several components of the stress field surrounding an atomic-scale flaw in the crystal structure of diamond. Led by Tokuyuki Teraji at Japan's National Institute for Materials Science, the team achieved its result using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, whose spin states respond differently to stress depending on how they are oriented relative to the stress field.

science.title: Tiny shifts in iron content tip a potential memory material between competing magnetic states
science.summary: A team of Yale researchers has figured out what gives a magnetic material its mysterious properties, a discovery that could help boost computing memory and the field of "spintronics." Their work is published in Physical Review Letters.

science.title: Thermal priming enhances heat tolerance and yield in tomatoes after recurrent heat stress
science.summary: High temperatures can significantly impair the growth and yield of crops, including tomatoes. A new study by an international research team led by Dr. Justyna Olas, of the Leibniz Institute for Horticultural Sciences (IGZ), has shown that tomatoes can respond better to subsequent heat stress following moderate heat exposure. The work is published in The Plant Journal.

science.title: An 'electron waiting room' helps blue titanium dioxide hold light energy longer
science.summary: To produce hydrogen using sunlight, the energy obtained from light must be retained until it can be used in a chemical reaction. However, if an electron that has gained energy from light quickly returns to its original position, it becomes difficult to make use of that energy.

The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

environment.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
environment.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

environment.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
environment.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

environment.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
environment.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

environment.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
environment.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

environment.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
environment.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

environment.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
environment.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.

mix_items.summary: Phase transitions are strongly constrained by spatial dimension. In conventional one-dimensional systems with short-range interactions, thermal fluctuations generally prevent continuous degrees of freedom from maintaining order over long distances.

mix_items.summary: The biggest international study ever on risky play has found that children who have more opportunities for outdoor adventurous play tend to have better physical and mental health, as well as improved social and cognitive development.

mix_items.title: NASA Invites Media to Moon Landing Simulation Experience in California
mix_items.summary: Members of the media are invited to tour a new lunar landing simulator at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley on Thursday, Oct. 29, and Friday, Oct. 30.

mix_items.title: Exploring how autism reduces sensitivity to feedback on decisions
mix_items.summary: Some people who have autism spectrum disorder struggle to adapt to changing demands in their environment. In a new study in JNeurosci, researchers discovered this struggle may be because these individuals are less sensitive to feedback about their behavior than individuals who do not have autism. This work was led by Nathaniel Zuk at Nottingham Trent University and Jaroslav Slobodskoy-Plusnin at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in collaboration with colleagues at University College London and Hebrew University.

mix_items.title: Chest 'digital twin' predicts light paths to help plan personalized pneumonia treatment
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) in Brazil and their international collaborators have created a computational model that can generate a "digital twin" of the human thorax. The goal is to personalize the treatment of respiratory diseases using a special type of light.

mix_items.title: Emotional content can improve how people process conversations
mix_items.summary: New in JNeurosci, Pyry Heikkinen and colleagues, from the University of Helsinki, explored how emotional meaning influences the way the human brain prioritizes information during naturally spoken conversations in a cocktail party setting.

mix_items.title: Laser-blasted plasma shows how instabilities could heat the sun's corona
mix_items.summary: From its visible surface, the sun radiates heat at a relatively cool temperature of 5,800 Kelvin. Yet within the thin outer layer of the sun's atmosphere known as the corona, electrons can reach temperatures of millions of degrees, for reasons astronomers have yet to fully explain.

mix_items.title: World-famous or local legend? New study investigates global and local forms of collective memory and group identity
mix_items.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte and Bernardo O'Higgins: two 19th-century military leaders renowned to this day in their native countries of France and Chile. Yet, while Napoleon's name and exploits are known throughout the world, O'Higgins remains largely obscure outside his homeland. This phenomenon demonstrates the distinction between global and local collective memory—the shared knowledge of the past that shapes group identity—and it is the topic of newly published research from Constructor University's Professor Dr. Mariana Macedo together with Dr. Melanie Oyarzun, Professor Dr. Cristian Candia and Professor Dr. César A. Hidalgo.

mix_items.title: Detailed brain map reveals how the insula shapes bodily sensations and processes pain
mix_items.summary: Tucked deep within the human brain's lateral fissure, beneath layers of the cerebral cortex, lies the insula. It is the hub that controls sensations ranging from pain and physical touch to hunger and emotions. Yet, it remains an enigma that neuroscientists have been trying to crack for ages. A recent study published in Nature has presented a new, detailed picture of certain regions of the insula that not only provides a new perspective but also questions some older ones.

mix_items.title: Lizard tail preserved in amber sheds light on a 100-million-year-old defense mechanism
mix_items.summary: A lizard making a dramatic escape, leaving its tail wriggling behind as it darts to safety, is an image familiar to many. Tail-shedding is one of the most widespread defenses against predators among living lizards, yet tracing the origins of this extraordinary ability has proved to be surprisingly difficult—how can we tell when this escape tactic first arose in lizards?

mix_items.title: Metabolic vulnerability identified in small cell lung cancer
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Cologne have demonstrated that, while various cellular states of small cell lung cancer are equally dependent on the amino acid cysteine, they react differently when deprived of it. While some cancer cells subsequently die via ferroptosis—a form of cell death in which harmful oxidized fats accumulate in the cell membranes—others undergo apoptosis, a controlled, programmed form of cell death.

mix_items.title: Wireless neural chip tracks brain changes in real time after Alzheimer's drug administration
mix_items.summary: A joint research team led by KAIST has used a small, implantable neural chip to wirelessly monitor real-time changes in a neurotransmitter involved in memory and learning after an Alzheimer's drug has been administered. In miniature pigs (minipigs), the team observed an increase in the neurotransmitter signal following drug administration, followed by a gradual return to baseline. The technology could help researchers assess how drugs act in the brain and develop stimulation methods that adapt to the brain's response.

mix_items.title: Reproductive health and cystic fibrosis: New guidance offers options and hope
mix_items.summary: For much of the history of cystic fibrosis (CF) care, reproductive health was not a major part of the conversation. Fertility challenges were the norm for men and women with this genetic disorder, and many grew up assuming biological parenthood was not possible.

mix_items.title: Britain's 1972 school reform may have lowered dementia diagnoses half a century later
mix_items.summary: A new study provides perhaps the strongest evidence yet that education can help mitigate long-term dementia risk.

mix_items.title: Black patients can face longer breast cancer care delays, study finds
mix_items.summary: Black patients and people with a learning disability face longer waiting times at key stages of breast cancer care, according to a nationwide study led by the University of Surrey.

mix_items.title: Japan's largest marine DNA study detects 126 fish species farther north than previously recorded
mix_items.summary: As climate change reshapes habitats both on land and at sea, you might go to the beach one day, only to find yourself in a place that looks nothing like you remember, around sea creatures you don't recognize.

mix_items.title: Armored amphibian lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago, fossils suggest
mix_items.summary: Scientists report fossil evidence of the first fully marine amphibian in a study from the University of California, Davis; Peking University; and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. The amphibian is an armored, giant salamander–sized, bottom-dwelling ocean creature that the researchers named Gerrothorax maritimus.

mix_items.title: AI-based computer model offers new weapon against hard-to-treat cancers
mix_items.summary: In a new paper published in Cell Reports Medicine, the UCL team outlines how they, in collaboration with a University of Cambridge team, developed a new type of treatment-predicting computer program that uses an individual's detailed genetic fingerprint to explore which treatments, if any, may kill their cancer—especially when standard treatments have failed.

mix_items.title: AI could help identify people at higher risk of common cancers using routine health data
mix_items.summary: Machine learning models using routinely collected health information, such as blood tests, medical history and lifestyle factors, could help identify people at higher risk of several common cancers, according to an international study reported at the ESMO Congress 2026.

mix_items.title: Immunotherapy combination extends survival in advanced endometrial cancer
mix_items.summary: An immunotherapy-based regimen combining durvalumab and the PARP inhibitor olaparib demonstrated encouraging long-term survival outcomes for patients with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer, according to new trial results presented by researchers from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Physicists reveal new paradigm for fiber growth in neurodegenerative diseases
mix_items.summary: Some proteins that are linked to neurodegenerative diseases can form both liquid droplets and amyloid fibers. But how are these two states connected, and where do the fibers grow? Leiden physicists Liru Feng and Louise Jawerth have discovered a counter-intuitive mechanism.

mix_items.title: An American startup wants to sell sunlight after dark. Who gets a say?
mix_items.summary: A U.S. startup has booked two Indian rocket launches to test a planned service no company has sold before: sunlight at night.

mix_items.title: Mapping the hidden global labor powering AI
mix_items.summary: Most people know by now that artificial intelligence powers much of the online world, sifting through social media posts, planning driving routes or helping to choose a movie to watch. But what goes largely unseen is the human labor—often performed by people working for low wages in the Global South—that makes this careful algorithmic lifestyle curation possible.

mix_items.title: NASA’s X-59 Aircraft and Test Pilot
mix_items.summary: NASA test pilot Mike Lippert poses for a photo ahead of his first time flying the agency’s X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft on Oct. 21, 2026. The X-59 has flown numerous times since its inaugural flight in November 2025; its first supersonic flight was on June 5, 2026. Lippert took off from NASA’s Armstrong Flight […]

mix_items.title: Remission achievable with usual care for axial spondyloarthritis
mix_items.summary: For patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA), remission is attainable with usual care, according to a study published in the Journal of Rheumatology.

mix_items.title: Sediment core reveals volcanic eruption preceded ancient cold spell by about 150 years
mix_items.summary: A new study led by an international research team including scientists at the University of South Carolina challenges the idea that the ancient Laacher See volcanic eruption in western Europe triggered a significant climate-cooling period affecting central Europe and the Arctic nearly 13,000 years ago.

mix_items.title: Heart drug combo reduces kidney damage in septic shock surgery, major trial finds
mix_items.summary: A simple adjustment to drugs given during operations for septic shock could prevent thousands of patients from suffering kidney damage, according to the results of a major trial now published in JAMA. Scientists from the University of Southampton working with experts from Zhejiang University School of Medicine in China discovered that combining the medications dobutamine and norepinephrine during surgery can significantly lower the risk of acute kidney injury.

mix_items.title: While some eucalypts are hard to kill, climate change may test the ability of others to survive
mix_items.summary: There's no tree like the humble eucalypt.

mix_items.title: Implantable device uses ultrasound to improve drug delivery to the brain
mix_items.summary: Patients with glioblastoma, an aggressive type of brain tumor, usually undergo surgery to remove the tumor. However, it's difficult for surgeons to remove all of the cancer cells, and the tumor often recurs.

mix_items.title: Stellar collisions may have been common when the universe was young
mix_items.summary: In our solar system's corner of the galaxy, stars rarely collide. It makes sense: Space is vast, and stars have room to roam. Even in most of the present-day universe, stellar collisions are rare. The James Webb Space Telescope, however, peers deep enough into space to see the universe as it was not too long after the Big Bang. Its observations have revealed extraordinarily compact stellar systems, raising the possibility that collisions between stars were once much more common.

mix_items.title: Patient-reported outcomes worse for patients with rheumatoid arthritis discontinuing TNF inhibitor
mix_items.summary: For patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), patient-reported outcomes (PROs) generally worsen shortly after tumor necrosis factor inhibitor (TNFi) discontinuation, according to a study published in the Journal of Rheumatology.

mix_items.title: Next-generation drug reduces endometrial cancer progression and death in trial
mix_items.summary: A new drug is effective at decreasing the recurrence of, and death from, endometrial cancer, an international study shows. The drug, called sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT), attaches to a protein on the surface of tumor cells and then delivers a targeted dose of a chemical that leads to cancer cell death.

mix_items.title: Plants may switch between reproductive strategies more easily than thought
mix_items.summary: When it comes to reproduction, plants have options. Some can fertilize themselves, while others rely on pollen from genetically different plants. Many populations even contain a mixture of both strategies. But scientists have long debated whether this mixed approach is truly stable or simply a temporary stage on the way from one reproductive strategy to another.

mix_items.title: Trust and inclusive language key to effective vaccination campaigns, report finds
mix_items.summary: Public health leaders should invest in long-term work with communities to develop trust and support more effective vaccination communications, according to a new report analyzing London's Why We Get Vaccinated campaign.

mix_items.title: Brain stimulation temporarily changes perception of sexualized images of women
mix_items.summary: Applying mild electrical stimulation to the brain temporarily removed a perceptual bias linked to the sexual objectification of women, in the first study of its kind. The study is published in the journal Social Neuroscience.

mix_items.title: RNA archiving method reveals what a cell did days ago
mix_items.summary: Information on what a cell did a few hours or days ago is generally unavailable to researchers, who can only measure the cell's current status. This is a problem if the aim is to understand how immune responses arise or why individual cancer cells survive treatment.

mix_items.title: Diamond defects confirm 80-year-old theory of crystal stress
mix_items.summary: For the first time, researchers in Japan have directly mapped several components of the stress field surrounding an atomic-scale flaw in the crystal structure of diamond. Led by Tokuyuki Teraji at Japan's National Institute for Materials Science, the team achieved its result using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, whose spin states respond differently to stress depending on how they are oriented relative to the stress field.

mix_items.title: Tiny shifts in iron content tip a potential memory material between competing magnetic states
mix_items.summary: A team of Yale researchers has figured out what gives a magnetic material its mysterious properties, a discovery that could help boost computing memory and the field of "spintronics." Their work is published in Physical Review Letters.

mix_items.title: Study finds links between low levels of lead exposure and strep throat in children
mix_items.summary: Even low levels of lead exposure can increase the risk of strep throat in children, according to new research from the University at Buffalo.

mix_items.title: Thermal priming enhances heat tolerance and yield in tomatoes after recurrent heat stress
mix_items.summary: High temperatures can significantly impair the growth and yield of crops, including tomatoes. A new study by an international research team led by Dr. Justyna Olas, of the Leibniz Institute for Horticultural Sciences (IGZ), has shown that tomatoes can respond better to subsequent heat stress following moderate heat exposure. The work is published in The Plant Journal.

mix_items.title: An 'electron waiting room' helps blue titanium dioxide hold light energy longer
mix_items.summary: To produce hydrogen using sunlight, the energy obtained from light must be retained until it can be used in a chemical reaction. However, if an electron that has gained energy from light quickly returns to its original position, it becomes difficult to make use of that energy.

mix_items.title: Most pregnancies after living kidney donation are uncomplicated, study finds
mix_items.summary: Most pregnancies after living kidney donation are uncomplicated, according to a new Canadian study that provides a clearer picture of pregnancy outcomes among kidney donors. The study, published in JAMA and led by researchers at Western University and London Health Sciences Center Research Institute (LHSCRI), compared pregnancies among living kidney donors in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia with those of women in similarly good health who had not donated.

mix_items.title: Five ways to look after yourself as winter approaches
mix_items.summary: When the clocks "fall back" in the fall, it signals the start of the winter months. And for many, this time change also signals the start of a difficult period—when the cold weather and long nights wear on their mental health.

mix_items.title: Treatment revives old liver cells in lab study, may help prevent Alzheimer's and heart disease
mix_items.summary: The liver's job of clearing harmful substances from the body is so essential that the organ may have implications for addressing unexpected diseases, including Alzheimer's and heart disease. A promising example comes from new Keck School of Medicine of USC research published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry.

mix_items.title: New zebrafish models could help test treatments for mental health conditions
mix_items.summary: A humble fish can experience features of mental health conditions such as schizophrenia and autism, raising the possibility that some of our most complex social behaviors may be more deeply encoded in our DNA than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Adding abiraterone to ADT and docetaxel improves survival in metastatic prostate cancer
mix_items.summary: Adding abiraterone to standard treatment provides a lasting survival benefit for men whose prostate cancer has already spread at diagnosis, reinforcing the value of early treatment intensification. The findings come from almost eight years of follow-up in the academically led phase 3 PEACE-1 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026.

mix_items.title: Omega-3 EPA linked to longer survival after surgery for colorectal cancer liver metastases
mix_items.summary: Patients assigned to receive high-dose eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), an omega-3 fatty acid, before and after surgery for colorectal cancer liver metastases had longer overall survival than those assigned to receive placebo, according to results of the phase 3 EMT2 trial presented at the ESMO Congress 2026, held in Madrid Oct. 23–27.

mix_items.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
mix_items.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

mix_items.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
mix_items.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

mix_items.title: As sand becomes more valuable, Sierra Leone’s Mahera Coast grows more vulnerable
mix_items.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — When the tide pulls away from the beach in the agricultural regions in Mahera in Lungi, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) across the sea from the country’s capital, Freetown, the digging commences. Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

mix_items.title: New Zealand builds an arsenal of tools to battle a ‘wily’ invasive seaweed
mix_items.summary: BAY OF ISLANDS, Aotearoa New Zealand — Since an invasive seaweed called caulerpa was discovered in Aotearoa New Zealand in 2021, forming meadows that blanketed parts of the seabed, it’s taken on an almost mythical status among people who spend time in coastal waters. “It’s so wily and so resilient,” Michele Rogalin-Henderson, a doctoral candidate […]

mix_items.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
mix_items.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

mix_items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
mix_items.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

mix_items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
mix_items.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

mix_items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
mix_items.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

mix_items.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
mix_items.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

mix_items.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.
